land.text: Anjou and Maine, 'given as an appanage to his brother Charles, Count of Provence' by Louis IX in August 1246
the counties of Provence and Forcalquier, left by Joanna I of Naples to Louis I of Anjou (adopted 1380); Charles of Naples disputed them in the Union of Aix (1382-1387)

successors.note: Cliopatria keeps the Capetian row to 1384 and starts the Valois-Anjou Provence shape in 1385; the Valois-Anjou dossier records the 1382 succession.

capitals.name: Angers
capitals.note: Infobox capital of the county of Anjou; the apanage stays under Angevin rule to 1290 but the seat of the House moves to Provence.

capitals.name: Aix-en-Provence
capitals.note: Infobox capital of the county of Provence: Aix. My reading for the dot: from 1251, when Arles and Avignon recognise Charles, the weight of the shape is Provence. Charles I was crowned king in Rome (1266) and the Angevin court sat at Naples; those seats belong to the Sicilian rows.

correction.text: Unchanged shape, to be drawn 1246-1250: Anjou and Maine, the apanage given to Charles of Anjou by Louis IX in August 1246

keyframe_review.note: 23,105 km2: Anjou and Maine (Maine-et-Loire, Mayenne, Sarthe and parts of Indre-et-Loire and Loir-et-Cher). 'Charles was invested in August 1246 by his brother Louis IX of France as Count of Anjou and Maine'; County of Anjou page: 'in August 1246 King Louis IX gave it as an appanage to his brother Charles'. Cliopatria starts the shape four years late; unchanged, drawn from August 1246. No infobox area on the pages opened, so Cliopatria's areas are unchecked against one.

correction.text: The 1260 shape of Anjou, Maine and Provence, drawn from the Provençal surrenders of 1251 (Forcalquier from November 1256)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1251-1258: the 1260 shape (Anjou, Maine and Provence) three years before its Cliopatria start. Charles became Count of Provence by marriage on 31 January 1246, but the first surrender is later: 'Arles was the first town to surrender to them in April 1251', Avignon accepted joint rule in May 1251 and Marseille sought peace in July 1252; Marseille's autonomy ended with his actions of 1252 and 1257 (Provence page); Forcalquier, given to his mother-in-law in 1248, was returned in November 1256.

correction.text: The 1260 shape plus the Piedmont communes that put themselves under Charles in 1259-1260 (Cuneo, Alba, Cherasco, Savigliano, with the lords of Mondovì, Ceva, Biandrate and Saluzzo as homagers); drawn 1259-1271

keyframe_review.note: 59,626 km2. Adds Piedmont: 'Sought Charles's protection against Asti in July 1259', the burghers of Cuneo asked him; Alba, Cherasco and Savigliano then acknowledged his rule and the rulers of Mondovì, Ceva, Biandrate and Saluzzo did homage. The shape holds only two Cuneo cells; the province is added, drawn from July 1259. The Drôme and Ardèche cells (the Rhône valley north of Orange, 42 cells that Cliopatria drops in 1272) are not Angevin on any page opened; the Provence page gives the marquisate north of the Durance to Alphonse of Poitiers until 1271 (after Alphonse of Poitiers died in 1271 Philip III inherited the marquisate, which he 'ceded ... in 1274 to Pope Gregory X to become the Comtat Venaissin'): kept as drawn, unverified: page budget.

correction.text: The 1272 shape plus the Piedmont lands, drawn 1272-1275, until the defeat at Col de Tende in early 1276

keyframe_review.note: 49,551 km2: Anjou, Maine and Provence with the Cuneo cells; the Drôme and Ardèche cells are gone. Right for 1272-1275 with Piedmont; the Piedmont losses begin in October 1274 (Vercelli and Alessandria joined the Ghibelline League) and end in early 1276 (Ghibelline forces defeated his troops at Col de Tende and the Angevins withdrew to Provence).

correction.text: The 1272 shape unchanged, Anjou, Maine and Provence, drawn 1276-1289, after the withdrawal from Piedmont

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1276-1289: the 1272 shape without Piedmont (the Cliopatria shape, kept as it stands: it holds two Cuneo cells that the page does not explain after 1276). The pages do not say what the Angevins kept in Piedmont after 1276.

correction.text: The 1326 shape unchanged, Provence and the Piedmont fragment, drawn from 1290: Anjou and Maine are Charles of Valois's

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1290-1325: the 1326 shape (Provence with the Piedmont fragment) from 1290. On 19 May 1290 at Senlis Charles II agreed to give his daughter Margaret to Charles of Valois, 'giving Anjou and Maine to him as her dowry'; she married him on 16 August 1290. Cliopatria keeps Anjou and Maine in this row to 1325 and starts a separate County of Anjou row (Valois) in 1294, so the two rows overlap for 1294-1325. The Capetian page's table dates the end of the title (Anjou 1299, Maine 1309), when Margaret died and the Valois line held the counties in their own right.

26,960 km2: Provence with the Piedmont fragment (Cuneo 3 cells, Turin 1). The pages date no change in 1326; it is the end of Cliopatria's overlap with the Valois County of Anjou row (1294-1332); the pages opened give no 1325 or 1326 event for Anjou or Maine. Nice is not in the shape; Provence page: 'This led, in 1388, to the separation of the city of Nice'.
26,960 km2, identical to 1326. The Provence page dates no border change in 1333-1374 ('In 1349, neighboring region of Dauphiné became a feudal possession' of the Valois is a neighbour's change).

correction.text: Unchanged shape, to be drawn 1375-1382: Provence and the Piedmont fragment under Joanna I of Naples

keyframe_review.note: 26,352 km2: drops the Turin cell and one Cuneo cell, unexplained by the pages (unverified: page budget). Right to 1382 only: 'in 1382, when she died, two pretenders claimed' Provence and Joanna I had adopted Louis I of Anjou in 1380; the Capetian row's 1383-1384 years belong to the Valois-Anjou dossier, which takes Provence in 1382.

region.text: Anjou and Maine, the apanage of Charles of Anjou

ledger.note: August 1246: Louis IX gives Anjou and Maine to his brother Charles, already Count of Provence by marriage (31 January 1246). 'Charles was invested in August 1246 by his brother Louis IX of France as Count of Anjou and Maine'; 'this meant Charles became Count of Provence in right of his wife'. The founding core drawn is the apanage: the Provençal towns recognise him from 1251.

region.text: the county of Provence, Arles first to surrender (without Forcalquier, which Beatrice of Savoy held until November 1256)

ledger.note: April 1251: Provence recognises Charles of Anjou. 'Arles was the first town to surrender to them in April 1251'; Avignon acknowledged joint rule in May 1251 and Marseille sought peace in July 1252. The county came to him by his marriage of 31 January 1246 (Beatrice); the Holy Roman Empire's fiefdom 'lasted until 1246' (Provence page). [Reviewer eu-10-g: the gazetteer's Provence includes Alpes-de-Haute-Provence (26 cells), which /ledger/2 gains in November 1256 (Forcalquier, returned by Beatrice of Savoy, Charles I page); subtracted here.]

region.text: Forcalquier, the northern county of the Provence inheritance (the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence)

ledger.note: November 1256: Forcalquier returned to Charles. He gave Forcalquier to his mother-in-law in 1248 and she returned it to him in November 1256 (Charles I page).

1257: Marseille's autonomy ends. The viscounty's independence 'only ended with the authoritative actions of Charles of Anjou in 1252 and 1257' (Provence page); the Charles I page has a coup in Marseille surrendering its political powers to his officials in the late 1250s.

region.text: Cuneo, Alba, Cherasco and Savigliano, with homage from Mondovì, Ceva, Biandrate and Saluzzo

ledger.counterpart: Communes of Piedmont (Cuneo, Alba, Cherasco, Savigliano)
ledger.note: July 1259: Cuneo asks for Charles's protection and Piedmont follows. 'Sought Charles's protection against Asti in July 1259'; Alba, Cherasco and Savigliano then acknowledged his rule and the rulers of Mondovì, Ceva, Biandrate and Saluzzo did homage. The page names the towns; the province is my reading.

region.text: Piedmont, lost to the Ghibelline League after Col de Tende

ledger.note: Early 1276: the Angevins withdraw from Piedmont. In October 1274 Charles named Robert II of Artois his deputy there, but Vercelli and Alessandria joined the Ghibelline League, and in early 1276 Ghibelline forces defeated his troops at Col de Tende and they withdrew to Provence (Charles I page). The page does not say what remained; Cliopatria keeps two Cuneo cells to 1382.

region.text: Anjou and Maine, the dowry of Margaret

ledger.note: 16 August 1290: Anjou and Maine go to Charles of Valois. 'giving Anjou and Maine to him as her dowry' (Treaty of Senlis, 19 May 1290; Margaret married Charles of Valois on 16 August 1290 at Corbeil); County of Anjou page: 'On 16 August 1290, the latter married his daughter Margaret, Countess of Anjou'. Cliopatria's Valois County of Anjou row starts in 1294.

region.text: Provence and Forcalquier (with the Piedmont fragment) at the death of Joanna I

ledger.note: 1382: Joanna I dies and Provence goes to Louis I of Anjou. 'Issueless Joanna I of Naples left the county to Louis I of Anjou of the House of Valois-Anjou' (Provence 1246-1382 in the page's table); Provence page: she adopted him in 1380 and 'in 1382, when she died, two pretenders claimed' the county, Charles of Naples's followers forming the Union of Aix (1382-1387).

wars.name: Charles of Anjou's subjugation of Provence
wars.outcome: Arles surrendered in April 1251, Avignon accepted joint rule in May 1251, Marseille sought peace in July 1252 and lost its autonomy by 1257; later revolts (Boniface of Castellane) are undated on the page.
wars.note: Avignon's joint rule is not in the Cliopatria shape; the Provence page dates Marseille 1252 and 1257.

wars.name: Angevin conquest and loss of Piedmont

zones.text: Cuneo and its neighbours, protected from Asti in July 1259 and abandoned after Col de Tende in early 1276

wars.outcome: Cuneo, Alba, Cherasco and Savigliano accepted Charles in 1259-1260; Vercelli and Alessandria joined the Ghibelline League in 1274 and Ghibelline forces beat his troops at Col de Tende in early 1276, forcing a withdrawal to Provence.

wars.name: War of the Sicilian Vespers
wars.outcome: The rebellion of 30 March 1282 ended Charles I's rule in Sicily; Boniface VIII confirmed the compromise at Anagni on 12 June 1295 and the Peace of Caltabellotta (1302) ended the war, Charles II giving up all rights to Sicily.
wars.note: Fought for Sicily and Naples, carried by the Sicilian dossiers; no French border of this row moved.

wars.name: Succession dispute for Provence (Union of Aix)
wars.outcome: On the death of Joanna I in 1382 Louis I of Anjou and Charles of Naples both claimed Provence; Charles's followers formed the Union of Aix (1382-1387); Nice separated under Savoy in 1388.
wars.note: Fought after this row's end year (1382); recorded in house-of-valois-anjou as the contest_start/contest_end pair.

certainty.note: Feudal frontiers of an apanage and a composite county; no treaty or survey lines on the pages. The Anjou/Maine boundary with Valois (1290) and the Provence boundary with Savoy at Nice (1388) are the datable exceptions.

notes: Merge test with house-of-anjou-sicily (shares Q939200): NOT merged. Both rows cite the dynasty article 'Capetian House of Anjou', but Cliopatria's 'Capetian House of Anjou' draws Anjou, Maine and Provence (France, with a Piedmont fragment) and 'House of Anjou-Sicily' draws Albania, Corfu and the Morea (Greece/Albania, 1272-1384); no land or government connects them except the dynasty (Charles I took the title King of Albania in February 1272 per the Charles I page, one of the Anjou-Sicily row's lands). They are different states; house-of-anjou-sicily (group eu-18) keeps its own dossier. Naples and Sicily are Cliopatria's kingdom-of-sicily and kingdom-of-naples rows. Overlaps to settle elsewhere: the Capetian row keeps Anjou and Maine to 1325 while Cliopatria's County of Anjou row (Valois) starts in 1294; this dossier ends the Capetian hold in 1290 (Treaty of Senlis; marriage of 16 August 1290) and the county-of-anjou dossier agrees (gain 1290). Cliopatria keeps the row to 1384; the dossier ends in 1382 (Joanna I) and house-of-valois-anjou records the 1382 gain. Not settled: what the Angevins kept in Piedmont after 1276 (the shape keeps two Cuneo cells to 1382); the Drôme/Ardèche/Vaucluse cells of the 1260 shape (the marquisate of Provence north of the Durance belonged to Alphonse of Poitiers to 1271, then to Philip III, who ceded it in 1274 to become the Comtat Venaissin); Avignon (joint rule from 1251) is outside the shape; the dates of Robert's and Joanna I's reigns were not on the pages opened, so no ruler strip is given. Pages thin: the Provence page has no area and no 1343 or 1309 dates. Counterparts without a dossier: County of Provence (pre-1246 Provence, imperial fief, infobox 1246-1487) needs a dossier from eu-10-x; Piedmont communes; Marseille.
